effect_node: Alveolar immune inflammation with fluid or pus
relation: Breathing difficulty and cough in pneumonia
quality_flags: K057S05: Open RN Respiratory Alterations → 6.7 Pneumonia → Overview → Pathophysiology; explicit causal description linking alveolar infection and inflammation with fluid or purulent filling to productive cough and difficulty breathing
independent_decision: Reassessed K057S02, K057S03, K057S04 and K057S05. K057S05 explicitly describes an inflammatory alveolar process with fluid or purulent accumulation resulting in productive cough and difficulty breathing. This supports the complete original LINK2 relationship as CAUSES at the level of a summarized clinical pathophysiology mechanism. K057S04 explains inflammatory mediator activation of airway cough pathways but does not independently establish the exact alveolar-fluid-to-composite-symptom transition. K057S02 lists the pathology and symptoms without an explicit causal explanation, while K057S03 directly explains dyspnea but not cough. These three sources remain partial and are excluded from supporting_source_ids. The evidence does not establish that fluid or pus alone causes cough or that every patient experiences both manifestations. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.

quality_flags: K046S01: CDC Health Effects of Cigarettes: Cardiovascular Disease → Smoking and cardiovascular disease; K046S02: NHLBI Smoking and Your Heart → Smoking Risks; Smoking and Heart Disease Risk
independent_decision: Independently reassessed K046S01 and K046S02. CDC directly states that smoking damages vascular lining cells and increases plaque buildup in blood vessels. NHLBI explains that tobacco chemicals damage blood vessels and promote inflammation and atherosclerosis. Both sources support Cigarette smoking → Atherosclerotic plaque buildup in arteries as a contributory CAUSES relationship. Not every smoker develops clinically significant atherosclerosis, and additional risk factors influence plaque development. This decision does not establish plaque formation in a particular artery or person. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.

quality_flags: SRC001: NHLBI Coronary Heart Disease Causes and Prevention → What causes coronary heart disease?; Plaque buildup
independent_decision: Independently reassessed SRC001. NHLBI explicitly identifies plaque buildup in the coronary arteries as the leading cause of coronary heart disease, also called coronary artery disease. This supports Atherosclerotic plaque buildup in arteries → Coronary artery disease as CAUSES when the plaque develops in coronary arteries. Plaque elsewhere in the arterial system does not by itself establish coronary artery disease. Coronary microvascular dysfunction and other mechanisms can also contribute to coronary heart disease. The existing SRC001 question-level source review remains independent of this link-specific decision. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.

quality_flags: K056S02: Ravimohan et al. → Pulmonary impairment after TB; Variability in lung function deficits; Airflow obstruction; Restrictive ventilatory defects; K056S03: Meghji et al. → The burden of PTLD; Causal pathways underlying PTLD; Heterogeneity of PTLD; Table 1
independent_decision: Independently reassessed K056S02 and K056S03. Ravimohan et al. describe associations between TB-related cavitation, fibrosis and bronchiectasis and persistent pulmonary impairment, with plausible but incompletely established causal mechanisms. Meghji et al. document residual structural abnormalities, impaired lung function and symptoms after tuberculosis, while emphasizing variation in clinical outcomes and uncertainty about causal pathways. Both sources support Lung tissue injury and scarring → Persistent respiratory limitation after tuberculosis as ASSOCIATED_WITH. They do not conclusively establish an independent CAUSES relationship for this exact intermediate and outcome. The associative relation is intentionally preserved rather than upgraded to pass a causal audit. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.
